A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WCDE identification and optimal-adjustment research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v3.

before.justification: v1 reports theoretical results, proofs, and illustrative causal graphs. Neither its main text nor appendices contain original empirical or simulation outcomes.

after.justification: v3 reports original simulations on two illustrative DAGs and the ASIA, SIGNALING, and MILDEW networks, with variance and MSE results in Tables 2–4 and D.2–D.3.

M1.justification: v3 adds a WCDE-specific AIPW estimation procedure in Equation (5.1), combining inverse-probability residual corrections with two marginal outcome-regression terms. This substantially extends v1's identifying-functional and influence-function framework into a concrete estimator. The O-set selection rule remains unchanged.

E1.justification: v1 has no empirical evaluation coverage. v3 adds simulations using the two existing illustrative DAGs and semi-synthetic network evaluations covering medical diagnosis (ASIA), protein signaling (SIGNALING), and crop disease management (MILDEW). These are newly evaluated scenarios, not new versions of earlier experiments.

E2.justification: v3 introduces empirical comparisons against alternative adjustment strategies using the same AIPW estimator. Table 2 compares the O-set with sets such as {G1,B2}, {G1,G2,B2}, and {B1,G2}; the network tables evaluate further competing sets. v1 discusses adjustment-set comparisons only theoretically. Cited methods such as CovSel and outcome-adaptive lasso are not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: v3 introduces variance/MSE evaluation, synthetic sample sizes from 250 to 2000, and network sample sizes from 250 to 10000. It specifies treatment contrasts using the two most frequent levels for multivalued treatments and restricted adjustment-set enumeration for large networks, yielding 112 MILDEW sets. These are new experimental protocols.

E4.justification: The new synthetic experiments test the four augmentation/pruning lemmas by adding outcome parents and removing redundant mediator or backdoor variables. Varying sample sizes and randomized nonlinear structural equations examines whether asymptotic variance advantages persist in finite samples. v1 contains the corresponding theoretical arguments but no empirical robustness or ablation evidence.

E5.justification: v3 newly specifies 50 randomized coefficient sets and 100 Monte Carlo replications per fixed synthetic setting in Appendix D.1. This adds basic repeated-run and variance-estimation reporting; confidence intervals, significance tests, and error bars are not introduced. v1 has no empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 2–4 and D.2–D.3 add entirely new numerical results. For example, Table 2 reports variance 0.0029 for {G1,G2} versus 0.0102 for {G1,B2} at n=250 in Figure 2's setting. Table 4 shows SIGNALING's {Erk,Mek,PKA} outperforming the O-set at small samples, with the O-set leading at n≥1000. These are new findings, not improvements over earlier measured performance.

T1.justification: Condition 2.3's explicit backdoor requirements become Condition 2.5's CDE-identification prerequisite. New Appendix A.1 supplies counterexamples to necessity claims and acknowledges that a complete CDE characterization remains unresolved. Appendix B.1 revises the identification proof, while Appendix C replaces graphical validity arguments for Lemmas 4.4–4.7 with functional-equality derivations. The influence-function formula and O-set theorem are retained.

C1.justification: v1 presents three theoretical contributions: identification, the influence function, and optimal adjustment. v3 adds a fourth contribution comprising an efficient AIPW estimator and numerical validation. Its abstract additionally claims lowest variance at practical sample sizes, extending the original emphasis on asymptotic optimality.

C2.justification: New Remark 2.3 explains the choice of marginal rather than confounder-conditional mediator weighting. v3 clarifies effects relative to observed mediators, excludes partial-mediator intervention settings from its scope, and discusses causal-discovery errors and finite-sample bias–variance behavior. Appendix A.1 also explicitly acknowledges the unresolved complete CDE identification criterion.

D1.justification: v3 adds nuisance-model specifications, including degree-5 splines with 10 knots, logistic regression, empirical frequencies, and Gaussian kernel density estimation. Appendix D documents coefficient distributions, transformations, noise, and MILDEW adjustment-set construction. A code repository link is newly supplied. v1 contains no comparable implementation or experimental reproduction information.

R1.justification: v3 adds supporting literature on AIPW, Bayesian-network benchmarks, CDE identification, and causal discovery. It also explicitly connects O-set optimality to the adjustment set returned by Maasch et al.'s local discovery procedure. The central positioning against existing ATE adjustment theory remains.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the introductory framing, condenses related work, and reorganizes Section 2 around separate estimand, validity, and adjustment-criterion definitions. Existing definitions and the identification example move into a reorganized appendix, and numbered Step subsections become compact paragraphs. The discussion is substantially expanded and separated into Section 6.

P2.justification: v3 adds experimental Tables 2–4 and D.2–D.3, the expanded partition Table A.1, and two counterexample diagrams in Figures A.1–A.2. v1's Figure 1 moves to Figure B.3; the partition and lemma diagrams are retained and renumbered. These additions and relocations substantially change the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves practical assessability through an explicit estimator, reproduction details, and finite-sample evidence showing both advantages and exceptions. Its counterexamples expose v1's CDE-necessity problem, and revised functional-equality proofs strengthen the adjustment-validity arguments. These gains extend beyond added content. Material limitations remain: Condition 2.5's complete CDE prerequisite is unresolved, and the abstract's broad finite-sample optimality wording exceeds what Table 4 supports.
